t: Feudalism bound lords and vassals by oaths of homage and fealty: the lord granted a fief, usually land, and the vassal owed military service, counsel and loyalty in return.
It grew as Carolingian royal power broke up in the 9th and 10th centuries, gave castle lords local power over peasants, and was abolished in France on the night of 4 August 1789.
Since Elizabeth A. R. Brown’s critique of 1974 and Susan Reynolds’s Fiefs and Vassals of 1994, historians have debated whether the term fits medieval Europe, let alone Japan.
dyk: Sark in the Channel Islands, settled in 1565 by Helier de Carteret under a charter from Elizabeth I and divided into forty tenements whose holders sat in its parliament, kept what was called Europe’s last feudal system until 2008.
ev: Under Charlemagne, grants of land to vassals in return for service become the usual reward of royal followers
Castles multiply in France as castellans seize rights of justice and taxation over the peasants around them
William the Conqueror has the landholders of England swear fealty to him at Salisbury
Minamoto no Yoritomo becomes shogun of Japan, ruling through vassals often compared with Europe’s
King John accepts Magna Carta, which limits the feudal dues a king may demand of his barons
Philip VI of France confiscates Gascony from his vassal Edward III of England; the Hundred Years’ War begins
On the night of 4 August the French National Assembly votes to abolish the feudal regime

f.power: A king or prince at the head of a hierarchy of lords and vassals, each lord exercising justice and command over the land and people granted to him
f.legitimacy: Oaths of homage and fealty, the grant of the fief, custom, and the Church’s teaching that society was ordered into those who pray, those who fight and those who work
f.chosen: Kingdoms and fiefs passed by inheritance; each heir did homage to his lord and paid a relief before taking possession, and a disloyal vassal could forfeit his fief
f.examples: Capetian France (987–1328), Anglo-Norman England (1066–1154), the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099–1291), the Holy Roman Empire, Japan under the Kamakura shogunate (1185–1333), by comparison
